meta.title: Male Reproductive System

blocks.x: The male reproductive system is composed of the testes, a system of genital ducts, the accessory sex glands (prostate gland, seminal vesicles, and bulbourethral/Cowper's glands), and the penis.

items: Testes — paired organs performing spermatogenesis (sperm production) and steroidogenesis (androgen synthesis)
Genital duct system — intratesticular ducts (tubuli recti, rete testis) and extratesticular ducts (efferent ductules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory ducts, urethra)
Accessory glands — prostate, seminal vesicles, bulbourethral glands — contribute the bulk of seminal fluid
Penis — copulatory organ, houses the penile urethra within its erectile tissue

blocks.x: Unlike the female system, the testis produces gametes continuously from puberty onward — a process that must protect genetically "foreign" haploid cells from the man's own immune system (the blood-testis barrier), transport immotile sperm through a long duct system to gain motility, and mix in secretions from three separate glands to form functional semen. This module moves from the testis outward: spermatogenesis, the duct system, the urethra and penis, and finally the accessory glands and semen.
How this module is organised
Testicular structure, seminiferous tubules, Sertoli and Leydig cells, the blood-testis barrier, and the full process of spermatogenesis.
The intratesticular and extratesticular duct system, the urethra, and the penis.
Prostate, seminal vesicles, bulbourethral glands, and the composition of semen.

items: Adult testes are paired ovoid organs lying within the scrotum, outside the body cavity
Cryptorchidism — failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum
Surrounded by a thick, dense CT capsule, the tunica albuginea
An inner loose CT layer, the tunica vasculosa, lies anterolaterally
Posteriorly, the tunica albuginea thickens and projects inward as the mediastinum testis
Each testis is divided into ~250 lobules by incomplete CT septa projecting from the capsule

blocks.x: Spermatogenesis — production of sperm (male gametes) Steroidogenesis — synthesis of androgens (sex hormones)
Each lobule contains 1–4 seminiferous tubules (where sperm are produced) and a connective tissue stroma containing Leydig (interstitial) cells.
The seminiferous tubule

Consists of a seminiferous epithelium (complex stratified/germinal epithelium), 30–70 cm long, 150–250 µm in diameter, surrounded by the tunica propria (peritubular tissue). Functions in both spermatogenesis and steroidogenesis.
The tunica (lamina) propria is multilayered CT containing 3–5 layers of myoid cells — flattened, contractile, peritubular cells that secrete the external lamina and fibrillar collagen.
Two populations of germinal epithelial cells

Regularly replicate and differentiate into mature sperm, derived from primordial germ cells. Organized in poorly defined layers of progressive maturity between adjacent Sertoli cells — spermatogonia (most immature, rest on the basal lamina) through spermatids (most mature, attached apically near the lumen).
Non-proliferating; slender, elongated cells with an oval nucleus and dark nucleolus; abundant cytoplasm extending from the basement membrane to the tubule lumen.
Functions of Sertoli cells

c: Support, protect, and nourish developing sperm (spermatids)
Phagocytose excess cytoplasm (residual bodies) from developing spermatids
Release mature sperm into the tubule lumen
Keeps testosterone levels high within the seminiferous tubules
Decreases FSH production by the anterior pituitary
Forms the barrier via tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells

blocks.x: Sertoli cells are columnar, extend from the basal lamina to the lumen, have a pale oval nucleus, and no longer undergo mitosis after puberty.
The blood-testis barrier (Sertoli cell barrier)

Lateral Sertoli cell membranes have long interdigitating processes enfolding clusters of developing spermatogenic cells. Near their bases, these interdigitations form tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) with adjacent Sertoli cells — dividing the tubule lumen into a basal and an adluminal compartment.

Spermatogonia and early primary spermatocytes are restricted to the basal compartment; more mature spermatocytes and spermatids sit in the adluminal compartment. New spermatocytes cross by formation of a new junctional complex beneath them, followed by breakdown of the junction above.
Leydig (interstitial) cells

Present between seminiferous tubules; endocrine cells that produce testosterone in response to luteinizing hormone (LH) from the pituitary. Testosterone is responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics and maintenance of the germinal epithelium. Leydig cells are cuboidal/oval, appear pale due to high cholesterol content, and often contain crystals of Reinke (function unknown).

A rise in gonadotropins shortly before puberty initiates spermatogenesis, which takes 65–75 days and proceeds in wavelike sequences of maturation — cycles of the seminiferous epithelium — rather than simultaneously throughout the testis, ensuring an even, continuous production of mature sperm.
Three phases
Differentiation of spermatogonia into primary spermatocytes, via mitosis (diploid).
Reduction division reduces the diploid chromosomal complement of primary spermatocytes to form haploid spermatids, via Meiosis I and Meiosis II.
Cytodifferentiation — transformation of haploid spermatids into spermatozoa.
Spermatocytogenesis in detail

c: Mitotically inactive reserve cells with dark nuclei; can resume mitosis to produce dark and pale type A cells
Pale-staining nucleus; mitotically active from puberty; give rise to more pale type A cells and type B spermatogonia
Undergo mitosis to give rise to primary spermatocytes
Large diploid cells; undergo the 1st meiotic (reductional) division to form secondary spermatocytes
Haploid; quickly undergo the 2nd meiotic division to form spermatids
Small haploid cells, located near the tubule lumen

blocks.x: The spermatogonial stem cell (SSC / type A spermatogonium) does not itself differentiate into a spermatocyte — instead it continues dividing into other spermatogonia or remains dormant, maintaining a reserve population.
Spermiogenesis — four stages

Granules accumulate in the spermatid's Golgi complexes, forming an acrosomal granule enclosed within an acrosomal vesicle, attached to the anterior end of the nuclear envelope. Centrioles migrate to the posterior pole to form the flagellar axoneme, then migrate back toward the nucleus to help form the tail's connecting piece.
The acrosomal vesicle expands over much of the nucleus, forming the acrosomal cap.

The nucleus condenses, flattens, and moves to the head region. Mitochondria aggregate around the proximal flagellum, forming the middle piece of the tail. The spermatid elongates, aided by a temporary microtubule cylinder called the manchette. Ends with the acrosome oriented toward the base of the tubule.

Loss of excess cytoplasm and the intercellular bridges connecting spermatids into a syncytium; discarded cytoplasm is phagocytosed by Sertoli cells. Ends when nonmotile spermatozoa are released (tail first) into the tubule lumen. Sperm remain immotile until they leave the epididymis, and become capacitated (able to fertilize) only within the female reproductive tract.
Sperm produced in the seminiferous tubules travel through a sequence of intratesticular and extratesticular ducts before ejaculation.

items: Straight tubules (tubuli recti)
Rete testis (in the mediastinum testis)
Proximal portion of the ductuli efferentes (efferent ductules)
Distal portion of efferent ductules
Ductus epididymis
Ductus (vas) deferens
Ejaculatory ducts
Urethra

blocks.x: Duct histology, in sequence
Proximal half lined by Sertoli cells; distal half lined by cuboidal cells (some bearing a single flagellum, possessing microvilli). Devoid of spermatogenic cells; no smooth muscle.

Irregular, anastomosing network of tubules within the mediastinum testis; highly vascularized; simple cuboidal epithelium with microvilli and a single luminal flagellum. Contains sperm; no smooth muscle. Conducts sperm from the tubuli recti to the efferent ductules.

Simple tall ciliated columnar cells alternating with short unciliated cuboidal cells, giving a saw-toothed luminal margin. Thin circular smooth muscle layer. Non-ciliated cells reabsorb testicular fluid; ciliated cells propel the still-immobile sperm toward the epididymis.

Pseudostratified columnar stereociliated (non-motile) epithelium; circular smooth muscle layer; smooth luminal margin. Two cell types: basal cells (round, precursors of principal cells) and principal cells (columnar, bear stereocilia). Stereocilia increase surface area for reabsorbing ~90% of luminal fluid. Head/body move sperm via peristaltic contraction; the tail is the principal storage reservoir. Muscularis thickens from 1 to 3 layers along its length.

30–45 cm long. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia; 3-layered muscularis (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal); 3 coats; star-shaped lumen; no muscularis mucosae or submucosa. Its dilated ampulla has a larger lumen, highly folded mucosa with glandular diverticula/crypts, simple columnar/cuboidal epithelium, and a comparatively thinner muscle layer.
Simple columnar epithelium; no smooth muscle/muscularis of its own — the fibromuscular tissue of the prostate substitutes for muscle.
Functions of the ductus epididymis

items: Temporary storage and maturation of sperm
Conducts sperm from the efferent ductules to the ductus deferens
Absorption of ~90% of tubular fluid via stereocilia cells
Phagocytoses residual cytoplasm and produces glycoprotein that inhibits premature capacitation

blocks.x: Newly produced sperm mature during passage through the epididymis, acquiring motility and fertilizing capacity. During this androgen-dependent maturation, the sperm head is modified by surface-associated decapacitation factor-containing glycoconjugates from epididymal fluid — a process called decapacitation (it must later be reversed via capacitation in the female tract).

The urethra is a fibromuscular tube conveying urine from the bladder to the exterior. In the male it also serves as the terminal duct of the genital system, running about 20 cm and passing through three distinct segments.
Male urethra — three segments

c: 3–4 cm, from the bladder neck through the prostate gland
~1 cm, from the prostate apex to the bulb of the penis, through the deep perineal pouch
Stratified or pseudostratified columnar; surrounded by skeletal muscle forming the external (voluntary) urethral sphincter
~15 cm, through the length of the penis, opening at the glans; surrounded by the corpus spongiosum
Stratified/pseudostratified columnar, except distally where it becomes stratified squamous continuous with penile skin

blocks.x: Ducts of the bulbourethral glands and the mucus-secreting urethral glands (glands of Littré) empty into the penile urethra along its length; the distal fossa navicularis is lined by stratified squamous epithelium.
Penile structure

items: Two corpora cavernosa — paired erectile masses; irregular vascular spaces lined by continuous endothelium, separated by connective tissue/smooth muscle trabeculae; vascular spaces shrink toward the periphery

Corpus spongiosum (corpus cavernosum urethrae) — single mass of erectile tissue with vascular spaces of uniform size; trabeculae richer in elastic fibers, less smooth muscle than the cavernosa; the penile urethra runs through its length
Tunica albuginea — thick fibrous CT sheath surrounding the paired corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum
Glans penis — dilated distal end of the corpus spongiosum, covered by the retractable prepuce (stratified squamous, lightly keratinized epithelium)
Median septum and trabeculae organize the erectile tissue internally, forming cavernous sinuses
Glands of Littré — mucus-secreting glands throughout the penile urethra

blocks.x: Erection mechanism
Semen (seminal fluid) contains fluid and sperm from the testis together with secretory products from the epididymis, ductus deferens, prostate, seminal vesicles, and bulbourethral glands.

items: Serves as the transport medium for sperm
Neutralizes the acidity of the male urethra and vaginal canal
Liquefies the coagulated semen
Activates the sperm after ejaculation

blocks.x: Prostate gland
Produces a clear/watery, slightly alkaline fluid rich in citric acid, prostatic acid phosphatase, amylase, fibrinolysin (liquefies semen), and prostate-specific antigen (PSA).

items: Simple or pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Prostatic acini/glandular alveoli in a fibromuscular CT stroma
No honeycomb appearance (distinguishing it from seminal vesicles)
Prostatic concretions (corpora amylacea) — increase in number with age; formed by precipitation of secretory material around cell fragments; may calcify

blocks.x: Seminal vesicles
Produce a whitish-yellow viscous fluid — accounting for about 70% of semen volume — containing fructose, fibrinogen, amino acids, ascorbic acid, and prostaglandins.

items: Honeycomb appearance — highly branched folds of mucosa
Pseudostratified columnar, low columnar, or cuboidal epithelium
Mucosal crypts
Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers; 3 coats

blocks.x: Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands
Produce a clear, mucous-like secretion that lubricates the penile urethra just prior to emission of semen. Contains galactose, galactosamine, galacturonic acid, sialic acid, and methylpentose.

items: Mucous glands with simple cuboidal or columnar epithelium
Surrounded by a fibroelastic capsule containing skeletal muscle
Connective tissue septa; CT capsule
